steps.say: Before an application can search a report, it needs the report's text in the order a person reads it.
A PDF stores pieces of text with their positions on the page. The reading order, the columns and the tables are left for the eye to see.
A program that reads straight across this page joins lines from the two columns.
One line then says that GDP growth rose to 51.3 percent of GDP. That figure is public debt, from the other column.
steps.speak: One line then says that G D P growth rose to fifty-one point three percent of G D P. That figure is public debt, from the other column.

steps.say: A search could return that line, and a model could repeat the wrong figure with a citation.
The preparation in this example reads the blocks of text column by column.
It drops the running footer and the page numbers, and keeps each heading with its paragraph.
The growth figure stays in its sentence, where the search can find it and a citation can point to it.
Tables need more care. Here each row keeps its label, so 6.7 stays with real GDP growth.
steps.speak: Tables need more care. Here each row keeps its label, so six point seven stays with real G D P growth.

steps.say: The title of the table, a baseline outlook in annual percent change, ended up in another passage.
A parser that reads tables as tables would keep the title, the unit and the year with every value.
